description: I am space enthusiast from India, i am working on earth analog problem to build a platform of tools where space mission scientists can find a better location on planet earth to analog their upcoming space mission, we are gonna provide them the locations earth which are very similar to mars and moon targeted bases according to different hyper parameters.
summary: Earth Analog Finder is an interactive dashboard that helps mission scientists find places on Earth that resemble a planned Moon base or Mars site. Users pick a target (Shackleton Crater, Marius Hills, Jezero, Gale and others), set priorities such as temperature, ground ice, geology and isolation, and receive a ranked list, map and gap analysis. It uses weighted similarity scoring, k-means analog classes and learned weights. We validated it against analog sites from NASA and other published sources: the ranking does not yet beat random, so we also show similarity against accessibility, helping scientists weigh trade-offs transparently before choosing where to rehearse.

Detailed Project Description

Earth Analog Finder is an interactive dashboard that helps mission scientists decide where on Earth to rehearse a Moon or Mars base. Space agencies test hardware, procedures and crews at analog sites such as Atacama, Devon Island or Hawaii, but no single place copies a lunar pole or a Martian crater, and the choice is often ad hoc.

How it works. The user picks a target (Shackleton Crater rim, Malapert Massif, Marius Hills lava-tube pit, Jezero, Gale, Arcadia Planitia, or a custom site) and sets what matters: temperature, day–night swing, rainfall, pressure, ground ice, basaltic geology and isolation. These come as a mission-purpose preset or as sliders, with optional hard constraints. The tool scales seven features, scores 32 curated Earth sites by weighted distance (euclidean, manhattan or chebyshev) and returns a 0–100 ranking, a world map, a radar chart and a per-feature breakdown that shows what each analog fails to replicate. K-means groups Earth into analog classes. Weights can be learned from known analogs, and a sensitivity test shows how stable the top five is.

Validation. We rebuilt a list of known analog sites from cited sources (NASA Facts, Apollo training records and published analog tables) and tested whether the ranking recovers them. It does not yet: known analogs rank better than random in 3 of 15 target and preset cases (6 of 15 with chebyshev distance), and 0 of 15 are statistically significant with euclidean (1 of 15 with chebyshev). Learned weights do not generalise either. For the Moon, the held-out mean rank is 18.3 against 16.5 for random picks. Our interpretation is that the score measures closeness to an environmental extreme, while real analog sites were often chosen for access and logistics. So the dashboard also plots similarity against accessibility with a Pareto front, letting scientists weigh the trade-off themselves.

Limitations. Earth cannot reproduce low gravity, vacuum or radiation. Earth-site values are approximate and still being verified, and the analog labels are few and noisy. Sites not named in any source, such as Ladakh Hanle in India, are candidates to examine, not validated analogs.

Built with Python, pandas, scikit-learn, Streamlit and Plotly.

NASA Data
No NASA datasets were downloaded or processed. We used the NASA Facts "Analogs" (2008) document to help build the validation labels, and the Moon and Mars target values are approximate figures informed by publicly reported mission results.

Space Agency Partner & Other Data
Analog labels come from the NASA Facts "Analogs" document, Wikipedia's "Terrestrial analogue site" and "Apollo program training" articles, the US National Park Service page on Craters of the Moon, Live Science and Europlanet. Full citations are in data/SOURCES.md. Earth-site feature values are approximate and hand-entered. A WorldClim cross-check script is included but was not run.

Use of Artificial Intelligence
Claude (Anthropic) generated the code, analysis scripts, documentation and presentation under our direction. No AI-generated images or video are used; the figures are screenshots of the running app.
